passages.t: Where quarrels come from, and the grace that is greater
passages.happening:
“What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you? You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask. And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures” (verses 1-3).

“You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God” (verse 4).

“Or do you think the Scripture says without reason that the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy? But He gives us more grace. This is why it says: ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with peace. Chapter 4 opens with war. James has warned that jealousy and selfish ambition bring disorder (3:16); now he shows it at work in the church: conflicts, quarrels, fights.

Where do they come from? Not first from circumstances or from other people, says James, but from inside: ‘the passions at war within you’. The word for ‘passions’ is hēdonē, from which English gets ‘hedonism’. It means desire for pleasure that has become a ruling power, demanding to be fed whatever the cost to others.

‘You kill and covet’ has puzzled readers. Some take it literally: in the years before the revolt against Rome in AD 66, Judea saw real violence, including killings by radical groups, and believers could be drawn into such passions. Others read it the way Jesus taught that anger toward a brother is close to murder. Others take the Greek to describe envy so fierce that it wishes a rival dead. The text does not settle it.

Then a surprising word about prayer. Some do not have because they never ask God. Others ask, but only to spend it on themselves. Prayer can be turned into one more way of feeding the passions.

“You adulteresses!” is a shock. James is not speaking to women only. He is using the prophets' picture of God's people as his bride, and of turning to other loves as unfaithfulness in marriage. The feminine form fits the picture: the whole covenant people is the wife. ‘Friendship’ in the ancient world meant sharing loyalties and enemies. To be ‘a friend of the world’, in James's sense, is to take the side of a way of life built on status, possessions and self-promotion, and so to stand against God.

Verse 5 is one of the hardest verses in the letter (see below). But verse 6 is clear. ‘He gives us more grace.’ However strong the pull of envy and the divided heart, God's grace is stronger. And he gives it to the humble.
passages.ot:
James quotes Proverbs: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (verse 6). Proverbs 3:34 in the BSB reads, “He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble”. The point is the same: God sets himself against pride and gives grace to the lowly.

The prophets often pictured Israel's turning to other gods as a wife's unfaithfulness. “But as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel” (Jeremiah 3:20). And God's answer was not only judgment but a promise: “So I will betroth you to Me forever” (Hosea 2:19).

The law calls God jealous for his people's love: “For you must not worship any other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14).
passages.hard:
What does verse 5 mean, and which Scripture is James quoting?

The words are not an exact quotation of any Old Testament verse. James may be summing up a theme of Scripture rather than quoting one verse, or quoting a writing now lost.

The Greek can be read two main ways. On one reading, God is the subject: God jealously longs for the spirit he placed in us, or for his own Spirit dwelling in us. This fits the Old Testament picture of God as a jealous God who will not share his people's love with idols, and it follows from the charge of unfaithfulness in verse 4. On the other reading, the human spirit is the subject: the spirit God placed in people tends toward envy. That fits the envy James has just described in verses 1 to 3.

Translations differ. The BSB capitalises ‘Spirit’ and makes the Spirit the one who yearns, a form of the first reading. Either way, verse 6 gives the answer: “But He gives us more grace”, enough for the pull of envy and for the divided heart.
passages.asks: Think of a conflict you are in now. Ask what you want in it that you are not getting. Ask whether you have prayed about it, and what you asked for. And ask where you have been a friend of the world's way of seeing, and what it would mean to come home.

passages.happening:
“Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded” (verses 7-8).

“Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
These four verses hold ten commands, one after another: submit, resist, draw near, cleanse, purify, grieve, mourn, weep, turn, humble yourselves. It is one of the strongest calls to repentance in the New Testament, and it sounds like the prophets of Israel.

The commands come with promises. Resist the devil, and he will flee. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Humble yourselves, and he will lift you up. James is not describing a God who waits with folded arms. He is describing a God who comes to meet those who turn.

‘Cleanse your hands’ speaks of what people do; ‘purify your hearts’ speaks of what they are inside. ‘Double-minded’ returns from 1:8: the two-souled person who wants God and the world at once. James calls them home.

‘Grieve, mourn, and weep’ uses the language of public repentance in Israel, when people fasted and wept over their sin. James is not telling believers that all laughter is wrong. He is speaking to people laughing carelessly while they quarrel, cheat and chase their pleasures. For them the right response is sorrow over sin.

And the last word is hope. ‘He will exalt you.’ The way up is down. Jesus said the same: ‘the one who humbles himself will be exalted’.
passages.ot:
‘Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you’ echoes the prophets' call: “‘Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you’” (Zechariah 1:3).

‘Clean hands and a pure heart’ come from the psalm: “He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to an idol or swear deceitfully” (Psalm 24:4).

The call to mourn echoes Joel: “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning” (Joel 2:12). And the promise to the humble is old: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).
passages.hard:
Does ‘Grieve, mourn, and weep’ mean that a Christian should always be sad, or that joy is suspect?

No. The same letter begins with ‘pure joy’ (1:2) and tells the cheerful to sing (5:13). James's call to mourn is aimed at a particular state: people living carelessly in sin, laughing while they quarrel and chase what they want. For them, the first step home is honest sorrow. That sorrow is not the end. It leads to God drawing near and lifting them up.

Some readers are the opposite: they already live under a weight of guilt that never lifts. This verse is not a call to add to that. Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Read the ten commands slowly. Ask which one you most need today. Ask whether there is sin you have been laughing off that calls for honest sorrow. And ask whether you believe that if you draw near to God, he will draw near to you.

passages.happening:
“Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it” (verse 11).

“There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
James comes back to the tongue. ‘Slander’ here means speaking against someone, running them down, usually behind their back. It was one of the ways the quarrels of verse 1 were being fought.

His argument is unexpected. The person who slanders a brother is also speaking against God's law, because the law says, ‘Love your neighbour as yourself’. By running down a brother, the slanderer acts as though that law did not apply to him. He sets himself above it, as its judge instead of its doer.

And there is only one judge. God gave the law, and God alone can save or destroy. When I set myself up to judge my neighbour, I am taking a seat that belongs to God.

James is not saying that wrong should never be named, or that the church must never correct anyone. Elsewhere he tells believers to bring back the one who wanders (5:19-20). He is speaking against the habit of tearing others down, the verdict passed in conversation, and the pride that thinks it stands above the law it uses on others.
passages.ot:
The law forbade slander: “You must not go about spreading slander among your people. You must not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:16).

The psalmist says that God will not put up with it: “Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence” (Psalm 101:5).

And Isaiah names God as the only true judge and lawgiver: “For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us” (Isaiah 33:22).
passages.hard:
Does ‘who are you to judge your neighbor?’ mean that no one may ever say that something is wrong, or report someone who has done harm?

No. James himself names sin plainly throughout this letter. And the rest of Scripture asks the church to tell the truth, to correct gently, and to protect the vulnerable. What James forbids is slander, tearing someone down, and the proud verdict that puts oneself above God's law.

This verse must never be used to silence someone who has been harmed. Telling the truth about abuse or wrongdoing is not slander. Abuse and other crimes are to be reported to the police and the proper authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you have spoken against this week, and whether you would have said it to their face. Ask where you have set yourself up as judge. And ask whether you can bring that person to the one Judge in prayer instead.

passages.happening:
“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.’ You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (verses 13-14).

“Instead, you ought to say, ‘If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.’ As it is, you boast in your proud intentions. All such boasting is evil. Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin” (verses 15-17).
passages.hearers:
‘Come now’ is a sharp way to get attention, and James will use it again in 5:1.

He pictures merchants. The Roman world had good roads and sea routes, and traders could move from city to city, set up for a season and move on. Jewish merchants were part of that network around the Mediterranean. James does not object to trade, to planning, or to making a profit. He objects to planning that leaves God out completely, as if tomorrow were theirs to command.

‘You are a mist.’ The word means a vapour or steam, like breath on a cold morning or mist that the sun burns off. Here for a little while, then gone.

So James gives them a better way to speak: ‘If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.’ This is not a magic phrase, and it is not fatalism, giving up and doing nothing. It is humility. Make plans, but hold them with an open hand before the God who holds your life.

The last verse sums up the letter's concern with doing. Sin is not only doing what is wrong. It is also failing to do the good you know you should. James's readers were planning their profits while, as chapter 5 will show, some of them were holding back other people's wages.
passages.ot:
Proverbs had said it long before: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1). And, “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

The psalms speak of life as a breath: “Let me know how fleeting my life is. You, indeed, have made my days as handbreadths, and my lifetime as nothing before You. Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath” (Psalm 39:4-5). The word ‘breath’ there, hevel, is the word that runs through Ecclesiastes.

And on the good left undone: “Do not withhold good from the deserving when it is within your power to act” (Proverbs 3:27).
passages.asks: Look at your plans for this year. Ask whether God is anywhere in them. Ask what you would change if you really believed your life is a mist. And ask what good you know you should do, and have not yet done.
